Posthumous Value of Digital Goods: Study Results

Does buying a photo as a legacy change how digital goods are valued relative to physical goods?

Author

Jamie C. Lee

Published

October 14, 2026

Summary

Research question. Atasoy and Morewedge (2018) found that people value digital goods less than physical goods. This study asks whether buying a good as a legacy for future generations changes that. The analysis is exploratory and asks three questions: is physical valued more than digital overall, is legacy valued more than lifetime overall, and does the legacy frame change the physical–digital gap (the interaction)?

  • Sample: 1,332 participants who finished the survey (329–337 per condition). WTP answers are right-skewed (median $25, mean $37.42, max $500); only 1.8% said $0.
  • 1. Physical vs. digital: a random physical-condition participant offered more than a random digital-condition participant 57.4% of the time (p < .001). Physical photos were valued about 28% more (log ANOVA p < .001). This replicates the digital discount.
  • 2. Legacy vs. lifetime: a random legacy-frame participant offered more than a random lifetime-frame participant 59.8% of the time (p < .001). The legacy frame raised WTP by about 38% (log ANOVA p < .001).
  • 3. Interaction: the physical–digital gap was smaller under the legacy frame (physical offered more 61.2% of the time under lifetime vs. 54.3% under legacy). The change is significant in the rank-based test (p .026) and not significant in the log ANOVA (p .087).
NoteNote on the analysis plan

The interaction is reported as the change in the physical–digital gap from the lifetime to the legacy frame, which matches the research question. (The power analysis described it the other way around, as whether the legacy effect is larger for digital than for physical.) All analyses are exploratory. The appendix walks through how each interaction test is computed.

Details and data quality checks follow. Section 4 has the full results and Section 5 the full ANOVA table.

1 Sample

  • Survey length: median completion time was 2.3 minutes (middle 50%: 1.7–3.2 minutes).
  • Children: 46.5% have children, 52.8% do not, 0.8% preferred not to answer. Among parents, 17.9% have grandchildren. Among non-parents, 26.2% plan to have children and 25.3% are not sure.

2 WTP descriptives

The mean is pulled up by a small number of very large answers (up to $500), so it is consistently higher than the median. That is why the planned tests use ranks (“who offered more”) rather than averages.

Round numbers dominate. The six most common answers ($20, $25, $50, $10, $5, $15) account for 66.7% of all responses. Many ties are expected with WTP and are handled by the rank-based tests.

3 Data quality

3.1 Open-ended explanations

How these were coded. Every one of the 1,332 explanations was read and coded against a fixed codebook (shown at the end of this section) by AI coders working from the full text plus each person’s condition and WTP. Keyword rules were not used to assign codes, because they cannot tell, for example, a correct contrast (“it’s not even a printed copy”) from a misreading (“I’d frame it on my wall” in the digital condition). To check consistency, a second, independent coder re-coded a random 150 responses (Table 4). Treat these codes as a careful first pass for you to verify, not as final judgments. Every flagged response is listed below with its full text.

Bottom line: 0 responses (0.0%) were off topic or nonsensical, so there is little sign of random answering. 65 (4.9%) were low effort (a generic phrase such as “seems fair” with no reason). In total, 119 responses (8.9%) carry at least one flag worth a look.

3.1.1 Themes in people’s reasoning

Patterns worth noting:

  • “I could take it myself” reasoning appears in 12.5% of digital explanations vs. 10.3% of physical ones, a small difference.
  • Durability or loss comes up in 9.2% (digital) vs. 9.3% (physical) of explanations, essentially the same. When people mention it, they speak directly to the mechanism the durability measure is meant to capture, so these responses are worth reading in the table below.
  • Future generations are mentioned by 13.7% of legacy-frame participants vs. 1.8% of lifetime-frame participants, suggesting the framing was noticed.

3.1.3 Browse all explanations

3.2 WTP page timing

The timer recorded four things on the scenario + WTP page: seconds until the first click, seconds until the last click, seconds until the participant clicked Next (page submit), and the number of clicks.

How fast is too fast? The page had 91 words in the lifetime conditions and 97 in the legacy conditions. At an average silent-reading speed (about 238 words per minute), reading it takes about 23–24 seconds. Even very fast skimming (500 words per minute) takes about 11–12 seconds. We use the skimming speed as the cutoff for “too fast to have read the scenario.”

The first click is not a good reading measure on its own. The distribution has two humps. About 47.1% of participants clicked within the skimming cutoff, many within 1–3 seconds. But 89.2% of these early clickers stayed on the page past the cutoff (median 18 seconds on the page). The most likely explanation is that they clicked into the answer box or on the page first, then read the scenario.

Page submit is the better test. Only 71 participants (5.3%) clicked Next before even a fast skimmer could have read the page; these are the responses most likely to be uninformed. A further 589 (44.2%) submitted faster than average reading speed, which is fast but not implausible for quick readers.

8 participants made no clicks at all on the page (e.g., used the keyboard), so they have no first or last click time.

3.2.1 Did response time differ across conditions?

How to interpret this.

  • Legacy-frame participants took longer, with no difference by good type and no interaction. Typical times were about 3.0 seconds longer to the last click and 3.3 seconds longer to page submit.
  • Part of that is just reading. The legacy scenario is 6 words longer, which should add about 1.5 seconds at average reading speed. The observed gap is larger than that, so the legacy framing may also have prompted somewhat more deliberation. Treat this as suggestive: the timer cannot separate reading from thinking.
  • What “last click” measures. On a page whose only answer is a text box, the last click is most likely the moment someone clicks into the box, often before they finish typing. 57.7% of participants made exactly one click. So the last click marks roughly when people started answering. Page submit includes typing and any second thoughts, so it is the closer measure of total time to produce a response.

4 Main analyses

Three tests, each run two ways:

  • Rank-based (primary): how often a participant in one group offered more than a participant in the other (probability of superiority, PS; 50% = no difference). This uses who outbid whom, so a few very large answers cannot dominate.
  • 2×2 ANOVA on log(WTP + 1): the familiar analysis. The log shrinks very large answers; estimates are converted to approximate percentage differences in WTP.

How to read each row:

  • Row 1: PS = probability a physical-condition participant offered more than a digital-condition participant. ANOVA: how much more physical was valued.
  • Row 2: PS = probability a legacy-frame participant offered more than a lifetime-frame participant. ANOVA: how much more legacy was valued.
  • Row 3: how much the physical–digital gap shrank under the legacy frame. In the rank version, the drop in the physical-over-digital PS; in the ANOVA, the drop in physical’s percentage premium.

In plain terms:

  1. Physical photos were valued more than digital ones (57.4% of comparisons; about 28% more), replicating the digital discount.
  2. The legacy frame raised WTP overall (59.8% of comparisons; about 38% more).
  3. The legacy frame shrank the digital discount, but how firmly depends on the analysis. The physical-over-digital advantage dropped from 61.2% (lifetime) to 54.3% (legacy). That change is significant in the rank-based test (p .026) and not significant in the log ANOVA (p .087). Treat it as promising but not yet conclusive.

What the interaction does and does not show. Under the legacy frame the gap was smaller, but physical was still valued somewhat more (54.3% of comparisons, p .052; about 17% more in the log ANOVA, p .035). So the legacy frame narrowed the digital discount. It did not reverse it, and a non-significant gap would not by itself show that the two are valued the same.

4.1 Follow-up comparisons

These break the 2×2 into its four simple comparisons, to show where the interaction comes from.

Where the interaction comes from. The legacy frame raised WTP for both goods (digital 62.8%, physical 57.1%), but more for digital, so the gap narrowed.

5 Full ANOVA table

6 Durability and ownership (exploratory)

Two questions: do durability and psychological ownership differ between the physical and digital photo, and do they differ between the lifetime and legacy frames?

6.1 Building the two indices

Do the seven items form two distinct indices? Yes.

  • Number of factors. A parallel analysis (which compares the data with random noise) suggests 2 factors.
  • Item loadings. In an exploratory factor analysis, every item loads strongly on its intended factor and near zero on the other (table below).
  • Model fit. A confirmatory two-factor model fits very well (CFI = 0.994, RMSEA = 0.053, SRMR = 0.023). Forcing all seven items onto one factor fits poorly (CFI = 0.542, RMSEA = 0.464).
  • The two constructs are related but distinct (correlation between factors = 0.48).

The items work the same way in every condition. The largest drop in CFI is -0.005, within the .01 standard, so comparing the conditions’ scores is legitimate.

Factor scores or simple averages? Both were computed. They are nearly identical: r = 0.994 for durability and r = 0.998 for ownership. The indices below use the simple average of the items (on the original 1–7 scale; α = 0.91 and 0.96), which is easier to interpret and compare across studies. As a check, the tests are also run on the factor scores.

6.2 Do the indices differ by good and by frame?

In plain terms:

  • Ownership: physical is clearly higher. People expected to feel much more ownership of a physical photo (6.32 vs. 5.66 on the 1–7 scale; all three tests p < .001). There was no overall difference between frames (p .644), but there was an interaction (p .005): the legacy frame slightly lowered ownership for the physical photo (6.42 → 6.22) and slightly raised it for the digital photo (5.59 → 5.73). This is the same direction as the WTP pattern, where the legacy frame narrowed the physical–digital gap.
  • Durability: at most a small, fragile difference. Physical was rated slightly more durable (5.54 vs. 5.40), but whether this is significant depends on the method: p .043 on the averaged index, p .008 on factor scores, and p .510 with the rank test. Treat it as not reliably different. There was no frame effect and no interaction.
  • Ceiling effects. 34.8% of participants gave the maximum ownership score (7) and 12.6% the maximum durability score, so these scales may understate real differences near the top.
  • Question order did not matter. Scores did not differ by whether durability or ownership was asked first (p .253 and .682).

Appendix: how the interaction tests are computed

This appendix walks through the two interaction tests in Table 8 using the study’s own numbers. Both start from the four groups: PL = physical × lifetime, PG = physical × legacy, DL = digital × lifetime, DG = digital × legacy.

The ANOVA interaction (on ln(WTP + 1))

Step 1: Transform each answer. Each WTP becomes ln(WTP + 1), the natural log of WTP plus one. The +1 keeps $0 answers usable, since the log of 0 is undefined. The log shrinks large answers ($500 becomes 6.2, $25 becomes 3.3, $5 becomes 1.8), so a few very large answers cannot dominate an average.

Step 2: Average the transformed values in each group.

Step 3: The physical–digital gap within each frame.

  • Lifetime gap = PL − DL = 3.200 − 2.863 = 0.338, so physical is about 40% higher.
  • Legacy gap = PG − DG = 3.430 − 3.273 = 0.157, so physical is about 17% higher.

A difference of x in natural logs converts to a percentage difference of e^x − 1. Strictly, the percentage applies to WTP + 1, but with typical answers of $15–$30 the +1 makes little difference.

Step 4: The interaction is the difference between the two gaps: 0.338 − 0.157 = 0.180. This “difference of differences” measures how much the physical premium shrank under the legacy frame.

Step 5: Measure the noise. People within the same group differ a lot (pooled standard deviation = 0.961 log units). Combining the uncertainty of all four group averages, the standard error of the interaction is 0.105. That is how much the estimate would typically vary if the study were repeated with new participants.

Step 6: Signal ÷ noise. t = 0.180 ÷ 0.105 = 1.71 (the F in the ANOVA table is t² = 2.93), giving p .087.

The rank-based interaction

This test never averages dollar amounts. It only asks: in a head-to-head matchup, who offered more?

Step 1: Pair everyone up. Compare every person in one group with every person in the other, and count how often the first group “wins.” Ties count as half a win. The result is the probability of superiority (PS).

Toy example. Physical buyers offered $10, $25, and $50; digital buyers offered $5, $25, and $30. That makes 3 × 3 = 9 matchups:

vs. $5 vs. $25 vs. $30
$10 win lose lose
$25 win tie lose
$50 win win win

Five wins and one tie: PS = (5 + 0.5) ÷ 9 = 61%. Only the order matters. $50 beating $30 counts the same as $500 beating $30 would, which is why extreme answers cannot dominate.

Step 2: Compute PS within each frame.

  • Lifetime (PL vs. DL, 110,873 matchups): physical wins 56.5% and ties 9.4%, so PS = 61.2%.
  • Legacy (PG vs. DG): physical wins 49.8% and ties 9.0%, so PS = 54.3%.

The many ties come from people answering round numbers.

Step 3: The interaction is the difference between the two PS values: 61.2% − 54.3% = 6.9 percentage points. Physical buyers’ head-to-head advantage over digital buyers dropped by this much under the legacy frame.

Step 4: Measure the noise. Each PS has its own standard error, computed with the DeLong method. Each person gets a score for the share of the other group they beat, and the more those scores vary, the less certain the PS. Here the lifetime SE is 2.16 points and the legacy SE is 2.22 points. The two frames involve different people, so their uncertainties combine as √(2.16² + 2.22²) = 3.10 points.

Step 5: Signal ÷ noise. z = 6.89 ÷ 3.10 = 2.22, giving p .026.

Why the two tests can disagree

They measure the interaction in different units.

  • The ANOVA asks whether physical’s percentage premium in typical WTP shrank (from about 40% to 17%). The size of differences matters, so variation among large answers adds noise.
  • The rank-based test asks whether physical buyers’ chance of outbidding digital buyers dropped (from 61.2% to 54.3%). Only who outbid whom matters.

Here both point the same way, but the change looked clearer on the rank scale.

Why not raw dollars? On the raw dollar scale there is essentially no interaction. The legacy frame added a similar dollar amount to both photos: average WTP rose from $26.47 to $40.77 for digital and from $34.80 to $47.55 for physical. So the dollar gap barely moved ($8.32 vs. $6.78). In relative terms, though, digital rose much more because it started lower (+54% vs. +37%). Whether the interaction exists therefore depends on whether “the gap” is measured in dollars or in relative terms. This report uses relative measures (log and rank), because the research question is about how the two formats are valued compared with each other, and “physical is worth 40% more” is more meaningful across products and price levels than “physical is worth $8 more.”

Appendix: coding procedure

The codebook given to every coder (verbatim) defined these codes:

  • quality: ok (gives a reason, even briefly), low_effort (generic, no reason, e.g. “seems reasonable”), off_topic (does not address the question, nonsensical, gibberish).
  • misread_format: the text shows the person believed they would receive the other format (or both). Contrasts such as “it’s not even a printed copy” do not count.
  • rejects_premise: refuses the scenario or says it does not apply to them.
  • wtp_text_conflict: the text clearly contradicts the WTP entered (e.g., “I’d pay $15–20” but entered $10). Mentioning other amounts as comparisons does not count.
  • sensitive: personal or distressing disclosures.
  • themes: zero or more of the ten themes shown in Figure 4.

Coders were told to choose ok/no when in doubt, so the flags are deliberately conservative. Codes are saved in wtp_explain_coding.csv (second-coder codes in wtp_explain_coding_reliability.csv), and the full codebook is in wtp_explain_codebook.md, all alongside this report.
